skill.name: ubiquitous-language
skill.description: Extract a DDD-style ubiquitous language glossary from the current conversation, flagging ambiguities and proposing canonical terms. Saves to UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md. Use when user wants to define domain terms, build a glossary, harden terminology, create a ubiquitous language, or mentions "domain model" or "DDD".
skill.summary: Turn domain discussions into a consistent glossary with canonical terms, relationships, examples, and flagged ambiguities.
skill.author: mattpocock

content.value_statement: Teams lose clarity when one concept has several names or one term has several meanings. This skill creates a canonical DDD glossary from your conversation.
actual_capabilities: Extracts domain-relevant nouns, verbs, and concepts from the current conversation.
Identifies ambiguous, overloaded, vague, and synonymous terms.
Selects canonical terms and lists aliases that teams should avoid.
Documents definitions, relationships, and cardinality in grouped Markdown tables.
Creates example dialogue that demonstrates precise domain language.
Updates UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md when later discussion changes the domain understanding.
limitations: Uses only the current conversation and an existing UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md file.
Cannot verify terminology with domain experts or external source material.
May propose incorrect canonical terms when conversation context is limited.
Rewrites UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md during updates, so existing content should be reviewed.

use_cases.title: Align a Product Team
use_cases.description: Convert planning discussions into shared definitions and flag terms that product, design, and engineering use differently.

use_cases.title: Clarify a Domain Model
use_cases.description: Document entities, lifecycle terms, relationships, and aliases before implementing a domain model.

use_cases.title: Maintain Project Terminology
use_cases.description: Update an existing glossary as requirements discussions introduce new concepts or refine previous definitions.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Basic Glossary
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a ubiquitous language glossary from this conversation. Define each important domain term and list aliases to avoid.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use after an initial domain discussion.

prompt_templates.title: Resolve Ambiguous Terms
prompt_templates.prompt: Review our discussion for ambiguous or overloaded terms. Choose canonical names, explain each distinction, and update the ubiquitous language glossary.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use when team members use conflicting terminology.

prompt_templates.title: Map Domain Relationships
prompt_templates.prompt: Extract our domain language and group terms by subdomain or lifecycle. Document relationships and cardinality where the conversation provides enough evidence.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use while refining a domain model.

prompt_templates.title: Evolve an Existing Glossary
prompt_templates.prompt: Read the existing UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md and incorporate this discussion. Revise changed definitions, add new terms, and recheck all flagged ambiguities.
prompt_templates.scenario: Use after requirements or domain understanding changes.

output_examples.input: We call organizations customers or accounts, while login identities are also called accounts.
output: Customer: An organization that purchases services. Avoid account.
User: An authentication identity. Avoid login and account.
Flagged ambiguity: Account refers to both Customer and User. Use the canonical terms instead.

output_examples.input: An order can ship in parts, and each completed shipment creates an invoice.
output: Order: A customer request to purchase one or more items.
Shipment: A dispatched group of items from one Order.
Invoice: A payment request created for a completed Shipment.
Relationship: One Order can produce multiple Shipments and multiple Invoices.

output_examples.input: Update our glossary after deciding that cancellation happens before dispatch, while return happens after delivery.
output: Cancellation: Termination of an Order or Shipment before dispatch.
Return: Movement of delivered goods back from the Customer.
Boundary: Use Cancellation before dispatch and Return after delivery.

best_practices: Include enough conversation context for definitions and boundaries to be evidence-based.
Ask domain experts to review canonical terms before the team adopts them.
Rerun the skill when requirements change or new ambiguities appear.
anti_patterns: Do not treat the generated glossary as verified domain authority.
Do not include generic programming terms unless they carry domain-specific meaning.
Do not preserve multiple synonyms when the team needs one canonical term.

faq.question: What does this skill create?
faq.answer: It creates UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md with definitions, aliases, relationships, example dialogue, and flagged ambiguities.

faq.question: What information does it analyze?
faq.answer: It analyzes the current conversation and reads an existing UBIQUITOUS_LANGUAGE.md file during later runs.

faq.question: Does it choose canonical terminology?
faq.answer: Yes. It selects preferred terms and lists conflicting synonyms as aliases to avoid.

faq.question: Can it organize terms by subdomain?
faq.answer: Yes. It creates separate groups when the conversation reveals clear subdomains, lifecycles, or actor categories.

faq.question: Will it update an existing glossary?
faq.answer: Yes. A later run can add terms, revise definitions, identify new ambiguities, and rewrite the example dialogue.

faq.question: Does it validate definitions with external sources?
faq.answer: No. It relies on conversation context, so domain experts should review important definitions and relationships.
